svg.title: How a node network-boots on OpenStack: iPXE is the node's root disk, and everything after it is unmodified OpenCHAMI
svg.desc: Nova only ever assigns a boot index to storage devices, so there is no way to put a NIC in a guest's boot order and no equivalent of libvirt's boot order of disk then network; the limitation is in how Nova generates the guest's XML, below the API, so no microversion, image property or policy change reaches it. The way round it is to make iPXE itself the storage device. Three commands do the whole of section 9: download ipxe.usb, an eight megabyte hybrid disk image carrying an MBR bootloader for BIOS and EFI slash BOOT slash BOOTX64.EFI for UEFI; upload it to Glance as a raw private image called och-ipxe-disk; and create each node instance from that image on its MAC-pinned port. The firmware then boots what looks to it like an ordinary disk, and from that point the chain is identical to real hardware and entirely unmodified OpenCHAMI. iPXE starts. CoreDHCP answers with the address SMD holds for that MAC and the lease carries the BSS URL. iPXE fetches the boot script BSS holds for that MAC. The Talos kernel and initramfs come from the head node's S3 store and boot into RAM. Talos enters maintenance mode and fetches its machine config from the talos.config URL on the kernel command line. Finally Talos selects its install disk by size rather than by device name and writes itself to the root disk, overwriting the iPXE bootloader — which is what stops the node network-booting again, with no state held anywhere. There is therefore no way-back command: the next boot is Talos from disk, re-provisioning is an openstack server rebuild, and the one capability given up is network-booting a node without destroying its disk. On real hardware all of this is one Redfish call setting the boot source override target to PXE, followed by a reset.
svg.text: §9 — a cloud has no “PXE” button, so we make iPXE the node's root disk
Amber is the part that exists only because this is a cloud — three commands, all of §9. Blue is ordinary, unmodified OpenCHAMI: identical on real hardware.
THE CONSTRAINT — WHY THIS SECTION EXISTS AT ALL
Nova only ever assigns a boot_index to storage. It cannot put a NIC in a guest's boot order, and the
limitation is in XML generation, below the API — no microversion or image property reaches it.
So we give it something other than the NIC to boot: a disk with iPXE on it.
On real hardware this is one call, not a section
BootSourceOverrideTarget=Pxe, then Reset. Everything
in amber is the hand-cranked equivalent of those two
Redfish fields.
THE OPENSTACK-SPECIFIC PART — ONE MECHANISM, THREE COMMANDS
No Cinder volume · no boot order · no rescue policy · no microversion · BIOS or UEFI from one file
§9.1 · GET THE ARTIFACT
A bootable disk image, 8 MB
MBR + SYSLINUX for BIOS, and a FAT partition
holding EFI/BOOT/BOOTX64.EFI for UEFI.
curl -fLO https://boot.ipxe.org/ipxe.usb
Not ipxe.iso — that is a CD, and we have no CD.
§9.2 · UPLOAD IT
A private raw image in Glance
Byte for byte, so Nova hands the guest exactly
the partition table the firmware needs to see.
image create --disk-format raw --private
hw_firmware_type must match §11's console=.
§9.3 · CREATE THE NODES
Root disk = iPXE
One instance per node, each on its MAC-pinned
port from §5.4. Nothing else is unusual.
server create --image och-ipxe-disk
This is the PXE button. There is no second step.
the firmware boots a plain disk — and from here nothing knows this is a cloud
UNMODIFIED OPENCHAMI — NOTHING BELOW HERE IS CLOUD-SPECIFIC
iPXE is running — from the node's own root disk
iPXE 2.0.0+ (ga1992) -- Open Source Network Boot Firmware
Only the 8 MB above this line is local. Everything below arrives over the wire,
which is why the boot chain proves something about OpenCHAMI at all.
CoreDHCP answers — §7.7, from SMD's record — §8
The address SMD holds for 52:54:00:be:ef:01, and the lease also carries the
BSS URL. A 172.16.0.2xx address is a bootloop lease — the MAC is unknown.
iPXE fetches its boot script from BSS — §11
http://172.16.0.254:8081/boot/v1/bootscript?mac=52:54:00:be:ef:01 … ok
Keyed on the MAC, so a node's role comes from its NIC — never from the Nova
instance name you typed. §8's offset-by-one port table matters here.
Talos kernel and initramfs, from the head's S3 — §10
:7070/boot-images/talos/vmlinuz-amd64 · initramfs-amd64.xz … ok
Booted into RAM. The root disk is untouched at this point and still holds iPXE —
that only changes at step 6, and that change is the whole design.
Maintenance mode, then the machine config
talos.config=http://172.16.0.254:7070/…/controlplane.yaml
No cloud-init, no SSH key, no user-data. The config arrives on the kernel
command line, which is what keeps OpenCHAMI the source of truth, not Nova.
Talos writes itself to the root disk — over iPXE — §10.6
diskSelector: { size: '>= 10GB' } — by description, never /dev/vda
This is the step that ends the network booting, by destroying the bootloader.
Install to any other disk and iPXE survives — and the node reinstalls for ever.
AND THE WAY BACK TO DISK BOOT — THERE ISN'T ONE, WHICH IS THE POINT
Nothing anywhere records “is this node provisioned?” — the disk answers it
Next boot — Talos, from its own disk
(nothing)
The bootloader iPXE lived in no longer exists, so
there is no command and no state to keep. §12.
Re-provision — start the node again
server rebuild --image och-ipxe-disk
Restores iPXE by wiping the disk — destructive,
deliberately. OVB uses the same mechanism.
What we gave up — and it is one thing
server rescue --image och-ipxe
Network-booting a node without wiping it. Matters
on metal, not at all here.
What is actually faked, and how little of it there is
Eight megabytes. iPXE is the only thing that comes off local storage. The node's identity comes from CoreDHCP reading SMD, its instructions from BSS, its operating
system from the head's S3 store and its configuration from a kernel argument — every one of them over the network, keyed on a MAC, exactly as on real hardware.
Both amber bands collapse to one Redfish call on real hardware — and the blue chain does not change at all. That is the whole claim this tutorial exists to test.
